turns.prompt_text: Are there any online Piano MIDI visualizers online I can play alongside my piano?
turns.response_html:
There are several high-quality, browser-based MIDI visualizers that use the Web MIDI API to connect directly to your digital piano without needing to download heavy software.

Since you're looking for something to play alongside in real-time, here are the most effective online tools:

Top Browser-Based MIDI Visualizers

  • Midiano (Best for Learning): This is one of the most robust web apps available. It provides a "falling notes" interface (similar to Synthesia) and can even generate sheet music from your MIDI input in real-time. It includes a GPU-accelerated particle engine if you want high-end visuals while you play.
  • Midee (Best for Aesthetics & Recording): Midee is a newer, open-source tool designed for "one-click" visuals. It focuses on a clean look with glow effects and particles. It’s particularly useful if you ever want to record a quick clip of your playing, as it can export 1080p video directly from your browser.
  • Chrome Music Lab: Piano Roll: If you want something ultra-minimalist and experimental, this is a great quick-start option. It’s built by Google and allows you to see your notes flow by in a classic piano-roll format with very low latency.
  • OnlinePianist: While primarily a virtual keyboard, its MIDI support is excellent for desktop browsers. It’s useful if you want a clear, traditional top-down view of the keys being pressed with letter labels or chord names visible.

Technical Requirements

To get these working smoothly with your piano, keep these two things in mind:

  1. Browser Compatibility: You must use a browser that supports the Web MIDI API. Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Opera are the most reliable. (Safari and Firefox have limited or no native support for this).
  2. Connection: Simply connect your piano to your computer via USB-MIDI or a MIDI-to-USB interface before opening the webpage. Most of these sites will prompt you for "MIDI Permission" as soon as they load.

The "Wildcard" Alternative

If you find that browser-based tools have too much latency for your specific setup, SeeMusic is a desktop application (Windows/macOS) that is widely considered the gold standard for real-time visualization. It offers much deeper 3D customization and lighting effects that react to your touch velocity.

Are you looking for a visualizer primarily to help with learning new songs, or are you more interested in the aesthetic/artistic side of the visuals?

That is a beautiful choice. "Clair de Lune" is a classic for a reason, but its complex timing and dense chords can be tricky to learn by ear or standard sheet music alone.

Using an online visualizer is a great way to map out those intricate movements. Here is the best way to get started:

1. Use Midiano’s Built-in Library (Easiest Method)

Midiano actually has "Clair de Lune" ready to go in its default catalog. This is the fastest way to start:

  • Launch the Song: Go to the Midiano "Songs" section and search for Debussy.
  • Play-Along Mode: I highly recommend toggling the "Wait for Note" feature (the person-shaped icon). Since this piece has many tempo changes (rubato), this mode will pause the falling bars until you strike the correct key on your piano, letting you learn at your own pace.
  • Visual Customization: You can adjust the "Falling Notes" speed and the zoom level of the keyboard to see the upcoming large chord jumps more clearly.

2. High-Quality MIDI Files to Download

If you want to use other visualizers like Midee or SeeMusic, you will need a high-quality MIDI file. Avoid "Easy Piano" versions if you want the full, lush sound of the original. Here are two reliable sources:

  • The Mutopia Project: This is a clean, public-domain MIDI based on the original 1905 Fromont publication. It’s "mathematically" precise, which is great for visualizers.
  • Alexander Peppe’s Piano Service: This version is sequenced specifically for high-end digital pianos and captures more of the dynamic nuance.

3. Practice Tips for Visual Learners

  • Isolate the Left Hand: "Clair de Lune" relies heavily on rolling arpeggios in the left hand. Most visualizers let you "mute" a track; try muting the right hand and just watching the left-hand patterns until the hand-leaps feel like muscle memory.
  • The 9/8 Time Signature: Because the piece is in 9/8, the visual "bars" might look different than a standard 4/4 pop song. If the visualizer allows it, turn on the Grid Lines to help you see where the "big" beats fall.

turns.prompt_text: I really enjoy playing piano along with Midiano, However, there are some changes I would like to make. I’m sure that I would be able to make my own custom version of that software using P5.jS
turns.response_html:
You can absolutely build a custom version of Midiano using p5.js. In fact, p5.js is an exceptional choice for this because its native 60fps draw() loop maps beautifully to the low-latency demands of real-time musical visualizers.

By combining the native browser Web MIDI API for input handling with the p5.js canvas for rendering, you can spin up a functional prototype surprisingly quickly.

Here is an architectural blueprint of how to structure a custom visualizer.

1. The Core Architecture

To make this work smoothly, your application needs to handle three core jobs:

  1. The Listener: Capturing raw MIDI events from your piano.
  2. The State: An array storing which notes are currently active, their timestamps, and their velocities.
  3. The Renderer: Translating pitch to the X-axis and time to the Y-axis.

The Coordinate Mapping

The fundamental logic of a "falling notes" display relies on simple coordinate translation:

  • X-Axis (Pitch): Map the standard 88-key piano MIDI numbers (21 to 108) across your canvas width.
  • Y-Axis (Time): The distance from the top of the screen represents time. For a live play-along, a note's height grows as long as the key is held down, and the entire block scrolls down the screen based on elapsed milliseconds.

2. A Minimal Boilerplate Setup

Here is a clean structural pattern showing how to bridge native Web MIDI access directly into the p5.js state engine without bloating your code with heavy external libraries.

let activeNotes = {}; // Keeps track of currently pressed keys
let fallingNotes = []; // Stores historical/scrolling note blocks
const SPEED = 0.2;     // Pixels per millisecond for scrolling

function setup() {
  createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight);
  setupMIDI();
}

function draw() {
  background(15, 15, 20); // Sleek dark mode background
  
  let now = millis();
  
  // 1. Update and draw falling notes
  for (let i = fallingNotes.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    let note = fallingNotes[i];
    
    // Calculate vertical position based on time elapsed
    let y = (now - note.startTime) * SPEED;
    let h = note.endTime ? (note.endTime - note.startTime) * SPEED : (now - note.startTime) * SPEED;
    
    // Map MIDI pitch (21-108) to screen width
    let x = map(note.pitch, 21, 108, 0, width);
    let w = width / 88;
    
    // Draw the note block
    fill(note.color);
    noStroke();
    rect(x, height - y - h, w, h, 4); // Renders moving upwards or downwards depending on preference
    
    // Clean up notes that have scrolled off-screen
    if (height - y + h < 0) {
      fallingNotes.splice(i, 1);
    }
  }
  
  // 2. Draw static interactive keyboard at the bottom
  drawKeyboard();
}

// --- Web MIDI API Integration ---
function setupMIDI() {
  if (navigator.requestMIDIAccess) {
    navigator.requestMIDIAccess().then(onMIDISuccess, onMIDIFailure);
  } else {
    console.error("Web MIDI not supported in this browser.");
  }
}

function onMIDISuccess(midiAccess) {
  for (let input of midiAccess.inputs.values()) {
    input.onmidimessage = handleMIDIMessage;
  }
}

function handleMIDIMessage(msg) {
  let [command, pitch, velocity] = msg.data;
  let now = millis();
  
  // Note On event (Key pressed)
  if (command === 144 && velocity > 0) {
    let newNote = {
      pitch: pitch,
      startTime: now,
      endTime: null,
      color: color(map(pitch, 21, 108, 100, 255), 150, 255) // Dynamic hue based on pitch
    };
    activeNotes[pitch] = newNote;
    fallingNotes.push(newNote);
  }
  
  // Note Off event (Key released)
  if (command === 128 || (command === 144 && velocity === 0)) {
    if (activeNotes[pitch]) {
      activeNotes[pitch].endTime = now;
      delete activeNotes[pitch];
    }
  }
}

function onMIDIFailure() {
  console.error("Could not access your MIDI devices.");
}

function drawKeyboard() {
  // Simple visualization for the piano keys at the base of the canvas
  fill(30);
  rect(0, height - 40, width, 40);
}

3. Taking it to the Next Level

Once you have the basic blocks scrolling smoothly, p5.js makes it incredibly simple to add advanced features that standard web tools lock behind menus:

  • Velocity-Based Particles: When a noteon message arrives, grab the velocity byte (0-127). You can use this to burst a custom p5.Vector particle system at the base of the key—hitting harder spawns faster, wider-spreading particles.
  • Shaders for the "Glow" Effect: Instead of using standard standard stroke(), you can load a custom WebGL vertex and fragment shader into p5.js to get that high-end, neon fluid-glow effect that apps like SeeMusic use.
  • Parsing MIDI Files: If you want to load a file (like a "Clair de Lune" MIDI track) to fall downward toward you while you play, look into the @tonejs/midi npm package. It parses raw .mid binary files into a clean JSON array of notes with exact timestamps, which you can push directly into your rendering loop.

Are you leaning toward building this purely as a visual canvas for your own live playing, or do you want to implement file parsing so you can read pre-recorded MIDI files down the screen?

turns.response_html:
That "odd rectangular port" on your piano is a standard USB Type-B port (historically used for printers, but universally used for digital instruments).

The brilliant thing about your cable setup—adapting it directly to USB-C—is that almost all modern keyboards are USB-MIDI Class-Compliant. This means they require absolutely zero custom software drivers. The moment you plug it into your computer, iPad, or phone, the operating system immediately recognizes it as a core audio/MIDI interface.

Here is a look at exactly how to read that data stream, how to send commands back to the piano, and a realistic roadmap of what we can get running right now.

1. Reading the Output: The 3-Byte Protocol

When you press a key on your piano, it doesn’t send an audio wave over that cable; it sends a tiny packet of digital data. For a standard key press, it sends exactly 3 bytes of data:

  1. The Status/Command Byte (What happened?): Tells the computer what type of action occurred and on what channel. 144 means a note was pressed down (Note On). 128 means a note was released (Note Off).
  2. The Data 1 Byte (Which key?): A number from 0 to 127 representing the exact pitch. A standard 88-key piano ranges from 21 (the lowest A) to 108 (the highest C). Middle C is always 60.
  3. The Data 2 Byte (How hard?): The Velocity, ranging from 0 (silent/released) to 127 (maximum force).

2. Sending Input: Can the Computer Talk Back?

Yes, absolutely. The connection is completely bidirectional. Through the browser's Web MIDI API, you can write a line of code that commands your physical piano to play a note.

If your piano has built-in speakers or sounds, you can send it a Note On instruction, and the physical keys' internal synthesizers will trigger. You can even send Program Change commands to programmatically change your piano's instrument patch (e.g., swapping it from a Grand Piano sound to an electric synth sound) right from your JavaScript code.

What We Can Achieve Tonight

  2. Open a Chromium-based browser (Chrome, Edge, or Brave) and go to Hardware Tester's MIDI Tool.
  3. Strike a few chords. You should instantly see your piano's name pop up at the top, along with a live rolling log of note numbers and velocities.

Step 2: Build a Live Visual Sandbox

Once the hardware tester confirms a connection, we can hop over to the online p5.js Web Editor and drop in a micro-sketch. We can write a script that opens the MIDI pipeline and maps your keys to visual elements instantly.

For example, we can make it so that striking a low note drops a massive, slow-moving ripple on the left side of your screen, while running up a high-pitched scale sparks a cluster of fast, bright particle bursts on the right.

turns.prompt_text: So I can get my MIDI to work correctly in the browser on my Mac Air. On my iPad, I cannot get it to work in the browser. However, I can get it to work on a app called Midi wrench
turns.response_html:
You just ran into one of the most infamous, long-standing roadblocks in web-based music development.

The good news is that your hardware, adapters, and cables are working perfectly—which you proved by getting a clean signal inside MIDI Wrench. The bad news is that you are fighting an underlying browser engine policy restriction on iPadOS.

Here is exactly why this is happening and how we can navigate it tonight.

The Culprit: WebKit vs. Chromium

The reason your Mac and iPad behave entirely differently comes down to how Apple manages its operating systems:

  • On your MacBook Air: When you use a browser like Chrome or Edge, you are running a Chromium engine. Chromium natively supports the Web MIDI API (navigator.requestMIDIAccess), allowing the web page to talk straight to your USB ports.
  • On your iPad: Apple's App Store policies dictate that every browser running on iPadOS must use Apple's WebKit engine underneath. Even if you download Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge from the iOS App Store, they are essentially just "skins" wrapped around Safari's WebKit engine.
  • The Apple Block: Apple explicitly stripped the Web MIDI API out of WebKit due to security concerns regarding hardware fingerprinting (the theory that malicious sites could identify your specific device based on the exact profile of connected MIDI gear). Because WebKit doesn't have the plumbing for Web MIDI, no mainstream iPad browser can talk to your piano.

Why MIDI Wrench Works

MIDI Wrench is a native iPadOS app. It completely bypasses the browser engine and communicates directly with Apple's CoreMIDI system framework, which has native, privileged access to the iPad's USB-C port.

How We Adapt Tonight

If you want to start writing code and customizing a visualizer tonight, here is the best tactical playbook:

1. Develop entirely on the MacBook Air

Since you are planning to build your own layout using p5.js, use the Mac Air as your primary workstation. You can spin up a local development server or use the online p5.js web editor inside Chrome. This gives you instant access to the console logs and allows you to read your incoming MIDI packets without jumping through security hoops.

2. The iPad Workaround (For later testing)

If your ultimate goal is to prop the iPad up on your piano music stand to display your custom p5.js visualizer, you can still do it using a specialized wrapper.

Go to the App Store and look for a utility called Web MIDI Browser (built by Takashi Mizuhiki). It is a barebones web browser engineered specifically to inject the Web MIDI API layer directly into an iOS web view. If you host your custom p5.js project on a local network IP or an https URL, opening that link inside Web MIDI Browser will allow your code to read your piano perfectly.

Let’s get this up and running on your MacBook Air right now.

To give you complete ownership of the code and set you up perfectly for your future GitHub repository, the best approach is to create a single local HTML file. You won't need to install any heavy development environments or servers—you can just write the code, save it, and double-click the file to open it instantly in Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge (which fully support the Web MIDI API on macOS).

Here is the complete, production-ready blueprint for your custom Midiano-style base, complete with a clean dark theme, responsive fullscreen scaling, and real-time canvas rendering.

Step 1: Create the Project File

  1. Open your text editor of choice on your Mac (like Neovim or VS Code).
  2. Create a new file named index.html.
  3. Copy and paste the entire block of code below into that file, then save it.
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Custom Piano MIDI Visualizer</title>
    <!-- Load p5.js via CDN -->
    <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/p5.js/1.9.0/p5.min.js"></script>
    <style>
        body {
            margin: 0;
            padding: 0;
            overflow: hidden;
            background-color: #0a0a0f;
            font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
        }
        /* Sleek overlay button for Fullscreen toggle */
        #fs-button {
            position: absolute;
            top: 20px;
            left: 20px;
            z-index: 10;
            background: rgba(40, 40, 55, 0.7);
            color: #ffffff;
            border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1);
            padding: 10px 16px;
            border-radius: 6px;
            cursor: pointer;
            backdrop-filter: blur(4px);
            transition: background 0.2s, transform 0.1s;
            font-weight: 500;
        }
        #fs-button:hover {
            background: rgba(60, 60, 80, 0.9);
        }
        #fs-button:active {
            transform: scale(0.95);
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>

    <button id="fs-button" onclick="toggleFullscreen()">🌌 Go Fullscreen</button>

    <script>
        let activeNotes = {};    // Tracks keys currently held down
        let fallingNotes = [];   // Stores historical/moving note blocks
        const SPEED = 0.3;       // Scrolling speed (pixels per millisecond)
        const KB_HEIGHT = 70;    // Height of the visual keyboard block at the bottom
        const TOTAL_KEYS = 88;
        const START_MIDI = 21;   // Lowest note on a standard piano (A0)
        const END_MIDI = 108;    // Highest note on a standard piano (C8)

        function setup() {
            createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight);
            setupMIDI();
        }

        function draw() {
            background(10, 10, 15); // Deep space-dark canvas
            let now = millis();
            let keyWidth = width / TOTAL_KEYS;

            // 1. Draw and update streaming note blocks
            for (let i = fallingNotes.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                let note = fallingNotes[i];
                
                // Track timestamps to calculate precise vertical positions
                let timeElapsedStart = now - note.startTime;
                let yStart = height - KB_HEIGHT - (timeElapsedStart * SPEED);
                
                let yEnd;
                if (note.endTime === null) {
                    // Key is still being held down; extend block completely to the keyboard
                    yEnd = height - KB_HEIGHT;
                } else {
                    let timeElapsedEnd = now - note.endTime;
                    yEnd = height - KB_HEIGHT - (timeElapsedEnd * SPEED);
                }
                
                let h = yEnd - yStart;
                let x = map(note.pitch, START_MIDI, END_MIDI, 0, width - keyWidth);

                // Draw the radiant note block
                fill(note.r, note.g, note.b);
                noStroke();
                rect(x, yStart, keyWidth - 1, h, 4); // Soft 4px corner rounding

                // Memory cleanup: remove notes that have completely floated off the top edge
                if (yEnd < 0) {
                    fallingNotes.splice(i, 1);
                }
            }

            // 2. Draw the Interactive Keyboard Base
            drawKeyboard(keyWidth);
        }

        function drawKeyboard(keyWidth) {
            // Draw baseline divider
            stroke(40, 40, 50);
            strokeWeight(2);
            line(0, height - KB_HEIGHT, width, height - KB_HEIGHT);

            // Draw a simplified representation of active visual keys
            for (let i = 0; i < TOTAL_KEYS; i++) {
                let currentPitch = START_MIDI + i;
                let x = i * keyWidth;
                
                if (activeNotes[currentPitch]) {
                    // Highlight the key if it's currently pressed down
                    let activeNote = activeNotes[currentPitch];
                    fill(activeNote.r, activeNote.g, activeNote.b, 150);
                } else {
                    fill(20, 20, 28);
                }
                stroke(30, 30, 38);
                strokeWeight(1);
                rect(x, height - KB_HEIGHT, keyWidth, KB_HEIGHT);
            }
        }

        // --- Window Optimization ---
        function windowResized() {
            resizeCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight);
        }

        function toggleFullscreen() {
            let fs = fullscreen();
            fullscreen(!fs);
        }

        // --- Native Web MIDI Pipeline ---
        function setupMIDI() {
            if (navigator.requestMIDIAccess) {
                navigator.requestMIDIAccess().then(onMIDISuccess, onMIDIFailure);
            } else {
                alert("Web MIDI API is not supported in this browser. Please use Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge.");
            }
        }

        function onMIDISuccess(midiAccess) {
            // Bind listener to all available incoming hardware ports
            for (let input of midiAccess.inputs.values()) {
                input.onmidimessage = handleMIDIMessage;
            }
        }

        function handleMIDIMessage(msg) {
            let [command, pitch, velocity] = msg.data;
            let now = millis();

            // Ignore data outside the standard 88-key piano boundaries
            if (pitch < START_MIDI || pitch > END_MIDI) return;

            // Note On command (Key Down)
            if (command === 144 && velocity > 0) {
                // Generate a vivid dynamic color mapping based on how high up the note is
                let hueValue = map(pitch, START_MIDI, END_MIDI, 0, 255);
                
                let newNote = {
                    pitch: pitch,
                    startTime: now,
                    endTime: null,
                    // Bright electric cyan-to-purple color gradient mapping
                    r: Math.floor(map(pitch, START_MIDI, END_MIDI, 0, 150)),
                    g: Math.floor(map(pitch, START_MIDI, END_MIDI, 200, 50)),
                    b: 255
                };
                
                activeNotes[pitch] = newNote;
                fallingNotes.push(newNote);
            }

            // Note Off command (Key Release)
            if (command === 128 || (command === 144 && velocity === 0)) {
                if (activeNotes[pitch]) {
                    activeNotes[pitch].endTime = now;
                    delete activeNotes[pitch];
                }
            }
        }

        function onMIDIFailure() {
            console.error("Critical Error: Web MIDI initialization failed.");
        }
    </script>
</body>
</html>

Step 2: Run and Test It

  1. Plug your piano’s cable chain directly into the USB-C port on your MacBook Air.
  2. Turn your piano on.
  3. Right-click your newly saved index.html file and open it with Google Chrome.
  4. Grant the browser permission to access MIDI devices if it prompts you.
  5. Hit the 🌌 Go Fullscreen button in the top left, strike a chord on your keyboard, and watch the notes stream up the display!

How the Coordinate Engine Works Here

Because you are playing live, the notes stream upward from the keyboard at the bottom of the screen. When you hit a key, a fresh block is generated right at the baseline. As long as your finger holds the key down, the top edge of the block climbs toward the sky while the bottom edge stays glued to the key. The second you lift your finger, the bottom edge breaks free and the entire block floats up into the vacuum of space.

When you play live, the raw MIDI stream from your keyboard is a single, flat data channel. But a pre-recorded MIDI file (.mid) is an entirely different beast.

Since Clair de Lune is defined by its soft, "moonlight" textures, I've added a PolySynth with a slightly softened attack to mimic a piano's felt hammers.

The Upgraded Audio-Visualizer

Overwrite your index.html with this version. It adds the volume slider, the synth engine, and schedules the audio to match the 3-second visual "lead-in" perfectly.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Debussy Performance Suite</title>
    <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/p5.js/1.9.0/p5.min.js"></script>
    <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/tone/14.8.49/Tone.js"></script>
    <script src="https://unpkg.com/@tonejs/midi"></script>
    <style>
        body { margin: 0; padding: 0; overflow: hidden; background-color: #050508; font-family: sans-serif; }
        .ui-container { 
            position: absolute; top: 20px; left: 20px; z-index: 10; 
            display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 15px;
            background: rgba(20, 20, 30, 0.6); padding: 15px; border-radius: 12px; backdrop-filter: blur(10px);
        }
        .controls { display: flex; gap: 10px; align-items: center; }
        button, input[type="file"]::file-selector-button {
            background: #34495e; color: white; border: none;
            padding: 10px 15px; border-radius: 6px; cursor: pointer;
        }
        #play-button { background: #27ae60; font-weight: bold; }
        .vol-label { color: white; font-size: 12px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1px; }
        input[type="range"] { cursor: pointer; width: 150px; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>

    <div class="ui-container">
        <div class="controls">
            <input type="file" id="file-upload" accept=".mid,.midi" />
            <button id="play-button" style="display:none;" onclick="startPerformance()">▶ PLAY PERFORMANCE</button>
        </div>
        <div class="controls">
            <span class="vol-label">Volume</span>
            <input type="range" id="volume-slider" min="-60" max="0" value="-12" step="1">
        </div>
    </div>

    <script>
        let activeNotes = {};    
        let fallingNotes = [];   
        let songNotes = [];      
        let songStartTime = 0;
        let isPlaying = false;
        
        // --- Audio Setup ---
        const synth = new Tone.PolySynth(Tone.Synth, {
            oscillator: { type: "sine" }, // Smooth, pure tone for Debussy
            envelope: { attack: 0.1, decay: 0.2, sustain: 0.6, release: 0.8 }
        }).toDestination();

        const SPEED = 0.35;       
        const KB_HEIGHT = 80;    
        const START_MIDI = 21;   
        const END_MIDI = 108;    
        const TOTAL_KEYS = 88;

        function setup() {
            createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight);
            setupMIDI();
            setupFileParser();
            
            // Volume Listener
            document.getElementById('volume-slider').addEventListener('input', (e) => {
                Tone.Destination.volume.value = e.target.value;
            });
        }

        function draw() {
            background(5, 5, 10); 
            let now = millis();
            let keyWidth = width / TOTAL_KEYS;

            if (isPlaying) {
                let currentSongTime = now - songStartTime;
                songNotes.forEach(note => {
                    let noteStartMs = note.time * 1000;
                    let yBottom = height - KB_HEIGHT - ((noteStartMs - currentSongTime) * SPEED);
                    let yTop = yBottom - ((note.duration * 1000) * SPEED);
                    
                    if (yBottom > 0 && yTop < height - KB_HEIGHT) {
                        let x = map(note.pitch, START_MIDI, END_MIDI, 0, width - keyWidth);
                        fill(note.color);
                        noStroke();
                        rect(x, yTop, keyWidth - 1, yBottom - yTop, 4);
                    }
                });
            }

            // Live User Input (Rising)
            for (let i = fallingNotes.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                let note = fallingNotes[i];
                let yStart = height - KB_HEIGHT - ((now - note.startTime) * SPEED);
                let yEnd = note.endTime === null ? height - KB_HEIGHT : height - KB_HEIGHT - ((now - note.endTime) * SPEED);
                let x = map(note.pitch, START_MIDI, END_MIDI, 0, width - keyWidth);
                fill(note.color);
                rect(x, yStart, keyWidth - 1, yEnd - yStart, 4);
                if (yEnd < 0) fallingNotes.splice(i, 1);
            }

            drawKeyboard(keyWidth);
        }

        async function startPerformance() {
            await Tone.start(); // Unlock audio context
            songStartTime = millis() + 3000; // 3-second visual lead-in
            
            // Schedule the Audio Performance
            songNotes.forEach(note => {
                Tone.Transport.schedule((time) => {
                    synth.triggerAttackRelease(
                        Tone.Frequency(note.pitch, "midi"), 
                        note.duration, 
                        time, 
                        note.velocity
                    );
                }, note.time + 3); // Sync with 3-second visual delay
            });

            Tone.Transport.start();
            isPlaying = true;
        }

        function setupFileParser() {
            document.getElementById('file-upload').addEventListener('change', async (e) => {
                const midi = await Midi.fromUrl(URL.createObjectURL(e.target.files[0]));
                songNotes = [];
                Tone.Transport.cancel(); // Clear old schedules

                midi.tracks.forEach((track, i) => {
                    if (track.notes.length === 0) return;
                     
                    let trackColor = (i === 1) ? color(0, 116, 217) : color(255, 65, 54);

                    track.notes.forEach(note => {
                        songNotes.push({
                            pitch: note.midi,
                            time: note.time,
                            duration: note.duration,
                            velocity: note.velocity,
                            color: trackColor
                        });
                    });
                });
                document.getElementById('play-button').style.display = 'block';
            });
        }

        function drawKeyboard(keyWidth) {
            stroke(30);
            for (let i = 0; i < TOTAL_KEYS; i++) {
                let pitch = START_MIDI + i;
                if (activeNotes[pitch]) fill(activeNotes[pitch].color);
                else fill([1,3,6,8,10].includes(pitch % 12) ? 15 : 40);
                rect(i * keyWidth, height - KB_HEIGHT, keyWidth, KB_HEIGHT);
            }
        }

        function setupMIDI() {
            navigator.requestMIDIAccess().then(m => {
                for (let i of m.inputs.values()) i.onmidimessage = (msg) => {
                    let [cmd, pitch, vel] = msg.data;
                    if (cmd === 144 && vel > 0) {
                        let c = pitch < 60 ? color(255, 65, 54) : color(0, 116, 217);
                        activeNotes[pitch] = { startTime: millis(), endTime: null, color: c };
                        fallingNotes.push(activeNotes[pitch]);
                        // Play live synth sound too!
                        synth.triggerAttack(Tone.Frequency(pitch, "midi"), Tone.now(), vel/127);
                    } else if (cmd === 128 || (cmd === 144 && vel === 0)) {
                        if (activeNotes[pitch]) { activeNotes[pitch].endTime = millis(); delete activeNotes[pitch]; }
                        synth.triggerRelease(Tone.Frequency(pitch, "midi"));
                    }
                };
            });
        }
        function windowResized() { resizeCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight); }
    </script>
</body>
</html>

Key Additions

  • Tone.Transport: This is the internal clock of the audio engine. .
  • Decibel Slider: Volume in Tone.js is measured in Decibels (dB). The slider goes from -60 (silent) to 0 (full volume). Setting the default to -12 gives you a comfortable starting point.
  • Live Feedback: I have also hooked your physical keyboard into the synth. Now, when you play along with the falling notes, your own piano strikes will also produce sound through your MacBook speakers, creating a "duet" with the recorded track.

The Wildcard Option

If the "Sine" wave synth feels too electronic for Debussy, you can replace the synth variable with a Reverb-heavy sound by adding this line right after the synth definition: const reverb = new Tone.Reverb(3).toDestination(); synth.connect(reverb);

That is a professional pivot. Moving from a single-file prototype to a modular repository will make it much easier to experiment with heavy features—like GPU shaders or recording capabilities—without breaking the core MIDI engine.

Since you're heading toward a Git-based workflow, here is a blueprint for how to decompose that monolithic index.html into a maintainable architecture.

Suggested Project Structure

To keep the logic clean, you can separate the concerns of Rendering (p5.js), Audio (Tone.js), and Hardware (Web MIDI).

/piano-visualizer
├── /assets
│   └── /samples          # Salamander Grand MP3 files
├── /src
│   ├── midi-engine.js    # Web MIDI API listeners & state management
│   ├── audio-engine.js   # Tone.js Sampler setup & Transport scheduling
│   ├── visualizer.js     # p5.js Draw loop & coordinate mapping
│   └── ui-manager.js     # Button handlers, volume sliders, and file parsing
├── index.html            # Main entry point (minimal boilerplate)
└── styles.css            # Layout and neon-blur effects

The Modular Roadmap (Branch Strategy)

Once you have the core moved into the structure above, here are three high-value extensions that work perfectly as standalone branches:

1. feature/particle-physics

Instead of just drawing rectangles, you can use a p5.js Particle System.

  • The Logic: When a noteOn event occurs, trigger a burst of 20-30 particles at the base of the key.
  • Modular Advantage: You can map the velocity from your piano to the particle speed and spread.

2. feature/gl-bloom-shaders

Standard p5.js rect() calls are CPU-bound. To get that high-end "glow" seen in professional apps, you can move the rendering to a WebGL fragment shader.

  • The Logic: Pass the activeNotes array as a uniform to a shader.
  • The Result: Real-time post-processing effects like bloom, motion blur, and neon trails without dropping the frame rate.

3. feature/learning-mode

This would implement the "Wait for Note" logic you see in Midiano.

  • The Logic: Pause the Tone.Transport whenever the currentTime reaches a note.time that hasn't been "validated" by a live MIDI input message.
  • The Result: A perfect tool for mastering the complex rubato sections of Clair de Lune.

Pushing to GitHub

When you're ready to initialize the repo, you can quickly stage your current progress. Since the Salamander Grand samples are hosted via CDN in the current code, your repo remains lightweight.

If you decide to download the samples locally to the /assets/samples folder later, just remember to add a .gitignore if you don't want to push several hundred megabytes of MP3s to your main branch.

To get the visuals branch rolling, run this in your terminal:

Since we’re shifting toward a modular architecture, the first step is to pull the p5.js drawing logic out of the main file and into a standalone module. This will keep the core engine lightweight while allowing us to experiment with heavy visual effects like particle systems or shaders.

1. Create src/visualizer.js

This module will handle the "Falling Notes" physics. I’ve added a velocity-based glow—meaning the faster/harder you strike a key, the more intense the "bloom" effect on that specific note block.

export class PianoVisualizer {
  constructor(p, config) {
    this.p = p; // p5 instance
    this.config = config;
    this.activeNotes = {};
    this.fallingNotes = [];
    this.speed = 0.35;
  }

  update(now, currentSongTime, isPlaying, songNotes) {
    // Logic for updating positions
    this.fallingNotes = this.fallingNotes.filter(note => {
      const yStart = this.p.height - this.config.kbHeight - ((now - note.startTime) * this.speed);
      const yEnd = note.endTime === null 
        ? this.p.height - this.config.kbHeight 
        : this.p.height - this.config.kbHeight - ((now - note.endTime) * this.speed);
      return yEnd > -200; // Keep notes slightly off-screen for smooth transitions
    });
  }

  draw(now, isPlaying, currentSongTime, songNotes) {
    const p = this.p;
    const keyWidth = p.width / this.config.totalKeys;

    // Render Song Notes (Downward)
    if (isPlaying) {
      songNotes.forEach(note => {
        const noteStartMs = note.time * 1000;
        const yBottom = p.height - this.config.kbHeight - ((noteStartMs - currentSongTime) * this.speed);
        const yTop = yBottom - ((note.duration * 1000) * this.speed);

        if (yBottom > 0 && yTop < p.height - this.config.kbHeight) {
          const x = p.map(note.pitch, this.config.startMidi, this.config.endMidi, 0, p.width - keyWidth);
          this.renderNote(x, yTop, keyWidth - 1, yBottom - yTop, note.color, note.velocity);
        }
      });
    }

    // Render Live Notes (Upward)
    this.fallingNotes.forEach(note => {
      const yStart = p.height - this.config.kbHeight - ((now - note.startTime) * this.speed);
      const yEnd = note.endTime === null 
        ? p.height - this.config.kbHeight 
        : p.height - this.config.kbHeight - ((now - note.endTime) * this.speed);
      
      const x = p.map(note.pitch, this.config.startMidi, this.config.endMidi, 0, p.width - keyWidth);
      this.renderNote(x, yStart, keyWidth - 1, yEnd - yStart, note.color, note.velocity || 1);
    });
  }

  renderNote(x, y, w, h, baseColor, velocity) {
    const p = this.p;
    // Layered glow effect based on velocity
    const alpha = p.map(velocity, 0, 1, 100, 255);
    
    p.noStroke();
    // Inner Glow
    p.fill(p.red(baseColor), p.green(baseColor), p.blue(baseColor), alpha * 0.3);
    p.rect(x - 2, y, w + 4, h, 6);
    
    // Core Note
    p.fill(baseColor);
    p.rect(x, y, w, h, 4);
  }
}

2. Update index.html to use Modules

You’ll need to add type="module" to your script tag to import this.

    kbHeight: 80,
    startMidi: 21,
    endMidi: 108,
    totalKeys: 88
  };

  let visualizer;

  new p5((p) => {
    p.setup = () => {
      p.createCanvas(p.windowWidth, p.windowHeight);
      visualizer = new PianoVisualizer(p, config);
      // ... rest of setup
    };

    p.draw = () => {
      p.background(5, 5, 12);
      const now = p.millis();
      visualizer.update(now);
      visualizer.draw(now);
      // ... draw keyboard
    };
  });
</script>

export class NoteParticle {
    constructor(p, x, y, color, velocity) {
        this.p = p;
        this.pos = p.createVector(x, y);
        // Velocity drives the initial "explosion" force
        this.vel = p5.Vector.random2D().mult(p.map(velocity, 0, 1, 2, 8));
        this.acc = p.createVector(0, 0.1); // Slight gravity
        this.lifespan = 255;
        this.color = color;

3. The WebGL Bloom Shader

To achieve a "neon bloom," we avoid CPU-heavy blurs. Instead, we use a fragment shader to calculate a glow around bright pixels. .

Create assets/bloom.frag:

precision mediump float;
varying vec2 vTexCoord;
uniform sampler2D tex0;
uniform float blurAmount;

void main() {
    vec4 color = texture2D(tex0, vTexCoord);
    vec4 bloom = vec4(0.0);
    
    // Simple 9-tap box blur for bloom effect
    for(float i = -2.0; i <= 2.0; i++) {
        for(float j = -2.0; j <= 2.0; j++) {
            bloom += texture2D(tex0, vTexCoord + vec2(i, j) * blurAmount);
        }
    }
    gl_FragColor = color + (bloom / 25.0) * 0.8;
}

1. The "Local Server" Requirement

Because the code now uses type="module" and loads external shader files, browsers like Chrome will block the request for security reasons if you just double-click the index.html file (the CORS policy).

Since you are on a Mac, the quickest fix is to run a tiny local server from your project directory. Open your terminal and run:

Then, navigate to http://localhost:8000 in Chrome.

2. The Missing Vertex Shader

In the previous step, we defined the Fragment Shader (.frag), but WebGL requires a Vertex Shader (.vert) to tell the GPU where to draw the coordinates. If this file is missing or empty, the shader will fail to compile.

Create assets/base.vert in your project:

attribute vec3 aPosition;
attribute vec2 aTexCoord;
varying vec2 vTexCoord;

void main() {
  vTexCoord = aTexCoord;
  vec4 positionVec4 = vec4(aPosition, 1.0);
  positionVec4.xy = positionVec4.xy * 2.0 - 1.0;
  gl_Position = positionVec4;
}

3. The WebGL Coordinate Shift

When you switch p5.js to WEBGL mode, the origin $(0,0)$ moves from the top-left corner to the center of the screen. This often makes everything "disappear" because your notes are being drawn relative to the old top-left coordinates.
